extracted.intended_audience: military administrators, quartermasters, Judge Advocate/ military legal officers, and War Department officials
extracted.subtask_description: Legal and administrative standards governing post/company exchanges, company/mess funds, custody of government property, and the WWII-era gratuity statute (Acts of May 11, 1908 and Mar. 3, 1909) including tests for line-of-duty/misconduct and beneficiary rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post exchange is government instrumentality — accounts subject to readjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: As the post exchange is an instrumentality of the Government and part of the military system of administration, accounts between the paymaster and the post exchange may be ordered readjusted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a post exchange functions as a government agency, financial interactions with paymasters can be reviewed and corrected by appropriate authorities. (C. 24167, Dec. 2, 1908.)

rubrics_metrics.name: "Proceedings" of post exchange council = majority record; minority report not binding
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph 318, Army Regulations, 1910 requires the proceedings of the post exchange council be submitted to the post commander for approval or objection; 'proceedings' means the record of action taken by a majority of the council.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A minority report may be appended but represents personal views and is not the 'proceedings' to be approved or disapproved; approval of only a minority report does not comply with the regulation. (C. 29268, Nov. 28, 1911.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Receipt of dividends when exchange officer dies — regimental adjutant may receive
rubrics_metrics.description: When a bank holding deposit in the name of the regimental exchange officer goes into receivership and the exchange officer dies before dividend declared, the regimental adjutant may properly receive and receipt for the dividends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to procedural handling of dividends in the event of officer death. (C. 16517, June 28, 1904.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Government may transfer property to post exchange at cost
rubrics_metrics.description: A bureau of the Government may legally transfer property to the post exchange at cost price since post exchanges are recognized by statute as Government agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports transfers between government bureaus and post exchanges without profit markup. (C. 20993, Jan. 26, 1907.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial telegraph costs not chargeable to public telegram appropriations
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost of telegraphic messages over commercial companies on post exchange business does not lawfully charge appropriations for public business telegrams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because post exchange is a government instrumentality, such messages should be sent free over lines owned/operated by the War Department. (C. 19479, Mar. 26, 1910.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability for paymaster overpayment when post exchange acted as paying agency
rubrics_metrics.description: If post exchange advances funds to a soldier and later receives a paymaster check which overpays due to paymaster error, the post exchange—having acted solely as the agency through which payment was made—is not liable; the soldier is debtor and the paymaster bears the loss under Army Regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the exchange officer relied on the paymaster's official check as final, loss from paymaster computational errors falls on the paymaster. (a. 7589, Jan. 28, 1900.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraud by steward of post exchange is a military offense
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the post exchange is part of Army administrative machinery established by regulations (which have force of law), fraud by the steward in management is a military offense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminal/military accountability applies to officers/employees of recognized post exchanges. (C. 5255, Nov. 15, 1898.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation for 'fuel and lights for enlisted men' includes canteen use but sales limited to officers
rubrics_metrics.description: An appropriation for fuel and lights for enlisted men includes fuel/lights required at a canteen, but where the statute authorizes sale of such articles for cash to 'officers' only, a sale to a canteen (for canteen use) is unauthorized even if canteen official is commissioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish authorized recipients (officers) from institutional uses (canteen). (P. 51, 239, Jan. 7, 1892.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Fuel allowance to post exchange must be certified and approved; applies to exchanges with laundries
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph 1051 (1904) / 1060 (1910) provides allowance of fuel to be issued to a post exchange must be certified by the officer in charge and approved by commanding officer; applies whether the exchange maintains a laundry or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certification/approval applies uniformly across exchange types. (G. 21521, May 13, 1907.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Post exchange profits may support a volunteer band (if organized by soldiers)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a volunteer band is organized by soldiers voluntarily (not statutorily recognized) but furnishes martial music for the post, it is proper to apply a portion of post exchange profits for support of the band.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible expenditure from profits when band benefits post morale and is soldier-organized. (C. 14893, July 1, 1903.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Volunteer band not entitled to 5% allotment of net profits
rubrics_metrics.description: A volunteer band is not entitled to share in the allotment of 5 percent of the net profits of a post exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies eligibility for statutory profit allotments. (C. 23870, May 24, 1911.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Officer boarding debt is debt to company fund; pay may be stopped
rubrics_metrics.description: A debt due from an officer to the company on account of boarding with the company is a debt to the company fund for which the officer's pay can be stopped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative remedy: stop pay to satisfy company fund debts. (C. 21595, May 31, 1907.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Receipt of percentage from private laundry does not create member debt for washing
rubrics_metrics.description: A private laundry's payment of a percentage of profits to a company fund does not make a washing charge owed by company members a debt to the company fund.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receiving profit does not convert underlying private-service charges into enforceable company-fund debts. (C. 21595, May 31, 1907.)

rubrics_metrics.name: No legal warrant for loans from company fund to enlisted men
rubrics_metrics.description: Advances from the company fund to enlisted men (e.g., to enable representation at athletic meets) are not warranted by law; company fund may not be used to loan money to enlisted men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Company fund disbursements must conform to authorized purposes; loans to enlisted men are unauthorized. (C. 23694, Aug. 6, 1908.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Company fund disbursed 'solely for the benefit of the company' — permissible purchases
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph 331 (1901/1910) requires company fund disbursement solely for the benefit of the company; purchases such as a typewriter, gardener or pool-room attendant wages, filing cabinet (if benefits men), and certain furniture for comfort/convenience are proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expenditures are allowed when reasonably construed as increasing comfort/pleasure/contentment/mental and physical improvement of the organization; but pay for duties that are official military duty (e.g., extra pay to a room orderly) is not proper. (C. 15447 and related citations; Circular No. 6, War Dept., Jan. 27, 1904; Circular 56, Oct. 31, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Company exchange has no official government status; company fund not liable for its debts
rubrics_metrics.description: An organization styled a company exchange that is not recognized by regulations has no official status as a government agency and is a civil association subject to merchant rules; the company fund will not be liable for the association's debts if no company fund was used in operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish recognized post exchanges (government agencies) from unofficial company-run exchanges. (C. 20279, Sept. 11, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Expense of bond for lost certificate may be paid from company fund
rubrics_metrics.description: If a certificate of deposit (dividend of a company) is lost without fault and the bank requires a bond to secure payment, the expense of obtaining such a bond may properly be paid from the company fund.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible administrative expense to protect company assets. (C. 14716, May 26, 1903.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary charge to recruits for laundry not authorized
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule requiring that a charge for washing be made against each recruit whether he sends clothes to be washed or not is without authority; similarly a company order requiring payment when clothes were not laundered is unauthorized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charges must reflect actual services rendered; cannot impose arbitrary mandatory fees. (C. 21900, Aug. 14, 1907; C. 23958, Oct. 15, 1908; C. 22627, Jan. 29, 1908.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Soldier on duty may bear arms despite state law prohibitions
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier on duty requiring him to bear arms may do so notwithstanding State or Territorial laws prohibiting carrying arms because he is an instrumentality of the U.S. Government and cannot lawfully be interfered with when performing duties properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While en route under orders the soldier's duty status permits bearing arms; compliance with private railroad rules that would require breaking guns or leaving them in baggage car would violate Army Regulations, and soldiers on duty should not be required to comply. (C. 3448 and related citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical practice by Army medical officers outside posts must conform to State law subject to military needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical practice by Officers of the Medical Corps outside military posts should conform to State laws, but treatment of active-list soldiers (an instrumentality of the U.S. government) cannot be controlled by State legislation when furnished where the soldier is stationed; attendance on families and civilians must comply with State laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retired enlisted men receive medical attendance at medical officer stations only; medical officers on duty are required to attend officers and enlisted men and, when practicable, their families. (Paragraphs 1450–1451; C. 3270, June 10, 1897; C. 20395, Sept. 18, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Company barber shops, billiards/pool revenues are part of company fund
rubrics_metrics.description: General Orders No. 28 (Feb. 28, 1911) authorized establishment of company barber shops and company billiard/pool tables, and revenues accrued are to be accounted as part of the company fund.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Official authorization of certain revenue-generating activities and accounting treatment. (C. 23694, June 27, 1911.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Band fund accounting follows regimental funds practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A band fund collected at a post for a volunteer band should be accounted for in the same way regimental funds are accounted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures consistent fiduciary handling of collective funds. (C. 23870, Sept. 16, 1910; Jan. 11, 1912.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Quartermaster's custody of deceased officer's effects requires extraordinary care
rubrics_metrics.description: When effects of a deceased officer are turned over to a quartermaster for shipment and are stolen while awaiting information, the quartermaster (having custody as part of official duty) must perform the duty without fault or negligence and with more than ordinary care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher standard of care imposed on quartermaster for personal effects, including cash and paymaster checks. (C. 9541, Apr. 29, 1901.)

rubrics_metrics.name: General mess fund subject to limitations similar to company fund
rubrics_metrics.description: Although not expressly stated, the general mess fund, being of similar character and treated together with the company fund in regulations, should be considered subject to similar limitations; e.g., erecting a house for a general mess dairy keeper is not a proper expenditure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disbursements must be for benefit of the mess members; capital expenditure for keeper's shelter not considered benefit. (C. 15407, Aug. 8, 1910.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive proclamation reserving public lands withdraws them from sale but does not suspend territorial laws absent Congressional modification
rubrics_metrics.description: An Executive proclamation reserving public lands for a military reservation withdraws them from sale, but Territorial laws in force continue to operate on the reservation unless Congress modifies their operation or exempts the reservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The President cannot place reservation beyond civil/criminal jurisdiction of insular courts where such control does not interfere with naval administration. (C. 12975, July 15, 1902.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Gratuity statute (Act of May 11, 1908): six months' extra pay to beneficiary; to be construed liberally
rubrics_metrics.description: Act grants six months' extra pay to beneficiary of officer/enlisted man who dies on active list; the act should be construed liberally as a gratuity with doubts resolved to benefit the beneficiary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After amendment (Mar. 3, 1909) the test is whether death was 'not the result of his own misconduct' rather than strictly 'line of duty.' (C. 25498 and related citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Test when several causes contribute to death (line-of-duty test)
rubrics_metrics.description: When several causes contribute to a disability resulting in death, some in line of duty and some not, the reasonable test is: if the disability not in line of duty would not have produced death independently of those contracted in line of duty, then the death is in line of duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to mixed-cause death determinations. (C. 23666, Nov. 19, 1908.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Death within reservation presumed in line of duty absent willful neglect or criminal conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a soldier dies within the limits of his reservation, in absence of evidence of willful neglect or criminal conduct, the death is in the line of duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presumption favors line-of-duty conclusion barring evidence to contrary. (C. 28666, Nov. 20 & Dec. 14, 1908.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-negligent accidental deaths while on pass can be in line of duty
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier not engaged in criminal/unlawful conduct and not exhibiting carelessness may die accidentally (e.g., knocked off a boulder) and such death is in the line of duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: soldier knocked off rock while watching breakers — death held accidental and in line of duty. (C. 23666 and listed dates.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Suicide due to own misconduct excludes gratuity; suicide due to insanity included
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier who kills himself by his own wrongful act (when sane) dies as a result of his own misconduct and is not in line of duty; but if suicide results from insanity, death is in line of duty absent evidence the insanity was incurred by soldier's fault or misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish sanity/insanity and causation; examples provided. (C. 23666 and related citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Injuries/death from athletic sports (baseball/football) are in line of duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Precedents demand injuries received playing baseball and football be deemed incurred in the line of duty; these manly sports are recognized as part of soldier life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: sergeant in charge of a football team who died in connection with the game was in line of duty. (C. 23666.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment (Mar. 3, 1909) changes gratuity test from 'line of duty' to 'not result of own misconduct'
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of Mar. 3, 1909 amends May 11, 1908 by striking 'contracted in the line of duty' and inserting 'not the result of his own misconduct'; this change means gratuity questions post-amendment depend on misconduct, not line-of-duty status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The amendment is prospective and applies to deaths after Mar. 3, 1909; legislative history indicates intent to change the test to misconduct-focused without altering original line-of-duty construction. (XV Comp. Dec. 896 and notes.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Widow/beneficiary designation rules under gratuity act
rubrics_metrics.description: If an officer/enlisted man dies leaving a widow, the widow receives six months' pay provided no other person was previously designated; unmarried men: pay to designated beneficiary; if no beneficiary designated, no gratuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no statutory obligation on soldier to designate a beneficiary; continuous service does not require re-designation; alternate beneficiaries are permitted. (C. 23666 et seq.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of troops covered by gratuity — Philippine Scouts and veterinarians included
rubrics_metrics.description: The gratuity of six months' pay may be paid to widows/beneficiaries of Philippine Scout officers/men and to veterinarians of Field Artillery and Cavalry — they are within the Army for gratuity purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies applicability across troop classifications. (C. 23666, Sept. 22 & Sept. 25, 1908.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous service: no need to re-designate beneficiary at each reenlistment
rubrics_metrics.description: Where service rendered is continuous, it is not necessary to make a new beneficiary designation at each new enlistment unless the soldier desires a change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative convenience; previous designation remains effective. (C. 23666, Nov. 13, 1908.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Suicide deemed misconduct unless competent evidence shows mental disability related to service
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier who commits suicide dies of an unlawful act and the death is generally considered the result of his own misconduct barring competent evidence he suffered a mental disability at the time and that disability was incident to or resulted from military service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burden to show insanity/mental disability sufficient to overcome presumption that suicide = misconduct. (C. 23666, June 8, 1910 and many follow-ups.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated acts constituting misconduct that bar gratuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the amended gratuity act, a variety of acts have been held to be 'misconduct' barring gratuity, including excessive alcohol use, drinking wood alcohol/bay rum/hair tonic, disobeying sentinel, absence without leave, trespassing on railroad track, attempting to board a moving train while on furlough, improper presence in house of prostitution, quarrels/assaults (with mistress, policeman, in saloon), being aggressor in a fight, escaping while a prisoner, standing up in rowboat causing capsize, unauthorized sailing in bad weather, drunkenness, and similar misconducts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List serves as precedent examples; each fact pattern examined to determine misconduct nexus to death. (C. 23666 and many dated decisions listed.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue of rations to destitute persons governed by Army Regulations; large-scale issues require Congress or presidential emergency action reported to Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: Issue of rations to destitute citizens follows Army Regulations; issuance to entire communities (e.g., fire, flood sufferers) can only be authorized by Congress; in emergency the President may act but should report to Congress; congressional relief funds cannot be used to reimburse private parties and similar rule applies to transportation reimbursements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restricts use of appropriations and establishes reporting/authorization channels for mass relief. (C. 7344 and related citations.)
